before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry. Critical and feminist geography add questions about capital, mobility, gender and contested place histories; Hayden and the History Workshop journal show specific historical uses. Driver examines the practices and disagreements of imperial geographical inquiry. Sauer’s historical reconstruction, Cosgrove’s criticism of visual neutrality and Febvre’s geographical collaborations reveal further disagreements within landscape inquiry.

before.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

before.label: Environmental history
before.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

representative_people.context: Argues that organisms accompanying Europeans helped transform environments and sustain settler expansion, particularly in temperate regions.
representative_people.works: Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986)

representative_people.context: Connects the Dust Bowl with agricultural capitalism as well as environmental conditions; this is a contested explanation, not the field’s unanimous account.
representative_people.works: Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); “The Dirty Thirties: A Study in Agricultural Capitalism” (1986)

representative_people.context: Brings feminist history of science into environmental inquiry; argues that mechanical conceptions of nature support new forms of control and capitalist development.
representative_people.works: The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980)

representative_people.context: Links colonial property and ecological change, city–hinterland commodity flows, and cultural ideas of wilderness. His later afterword criticizes schematic capitalism and uneven treatment of Indigenous and colonial sources in his first book.
representative_people.works: Changes in the Land (1983); Nature’s Metropolis (1991); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995)

representative_people.context: Ecological observation and conservation ethics precede the field’s later consolidation; Cronon identifies a landscape-training model drawn from Leopold.

representative_people.works: With Ramachandra Guha, This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India (1992; UC Press edition 1993)

representative_people.context: Traces conservation ideas through colonial island settings and scientific networks; his geographical emphasis differs from histories of mainland African conservation.

representative_people.context: Examines South African conservation through the politics of Kruger National Park, racial power and Afrikaner nationalism.
representative_people.works: The Kruger National Park: A Social and Political History (1995)

before.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship.

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.

after.label: Environmental history

before.label: History Workshop movement
before.description: Develops collaborative history from below through adult education, labour movements, and historical scholarship. added.title: Robert D. Bullard, Dumping in Dixie: Race, Class, and Environmental Quality (1990), excerpt reprinted in American Earth (2008), 725–736.
added.citation: Robert D. Bullard, Dumping in Dixie: Race, Class, and Environmental Quality (1990), excerpt reprinted in American Earth (2008), 725–736.

verification.note: Complete available Bullard excerpt and its notes read in local OCR across seven double-page scan images; Alsen opening 732–733 visually checked. The excerpt includes introductory argument and the Alsen case, not the full book or all five cases. Adjacent McKibben ending, editorial biography and Adams image are separate material. Original 1990 publication corroborated by https://books.google.com/books/about/Dumping_In_Dixie.html?id=cHWmAAAAIAAJ . Later reprint is not a new mapped intervention. Bullard distinguishes concern from capacity to act, links race/class and environmental burdens, and records disagreement within Alsen about settlement and health provision. Interviews, epidemiological claims, statistics and legal files not independently checked. Quotations from Morris and citations of Beverly H. Wright establish named resources, not fresh readings of those works.

added.title: Rita Huggins and Jackie Huggins, Auntie Rita (1994), publisher descriptions of the original work and later editions.
added.citation: Rita Huggins and Jackie Huggins, Auntie Rita (1994), publisher descriptions of the original work and later editions.

verification.note: AIATSIS description and contributor credits read; page dates its edition 2005. Aboriginal Studies Press distributor https://newsouthbooks.com.au/books/auntie-rita/ confirms original 1994 and revised 2023 edition, two voices, Rita’s displacement from Bidjara/Bidyara Country and Jackie’s Bidjara/Birri Gubba Juru identification. Google Books original/reprint record corroborates 1994. Primary sample, contents and foreword links failed web; sample returned 403 locally and outside sandbox. OverDrive 1994-labelled listing has an empty sample URL. Thus book body unread, no new-edition passages backdated and no claim of comprehensive interpretation. Specific biographical details follow publisher descriptions; the authors’ distinct voices are retained.

added.title: Anita Heiss, review of Jackie Huggins, Sister Girl, Australian Humanities Review (December 1998).
added.citation: Anita Heiss, review of Jackie Huggins, Sister Girl, Australian Humanities Review (December 1998).

verification.note: Complete published review read. Heiss discusses Huggins’s account of writing her mother’s life, oral testimony, women’s labor, white feminism and a return to Kooramindanjie. This is a named contemporary critical reception, not direct reading of Sister Girl or Kooramindanjie. Her anticipated curricular use is a prediction, not verified teaching adoption; her guess about the hooks interview date is not used as chronology. Claims of being first of a kind and generalizations about all Aboriginal perspectives are not adopted. Review’s own identification of Heiss as Wiradjuri is explicit.

outcomes.finding: Bullard’s introduction and Alsen excerpt add unequal pollution burdens, organizing capacity and internal disagreement. Rita and Jackie Huggins’s 1994 life-history project supplies a situated comparison about Country, displacement and historical voice. Their 1995 place article with Jane M. Jacobs establishes specific collaborative publication in History Workshop; a public archival description corroborates the project. Heiss’s 1998 review supplies named reception of Jackie Huggins’s reflections on oral testimony and historical authority. These resources are compared with existing Cronon and Carruthers selections without inferring direct influence.
outcomes.research_limit: Bullard excerpt and notes read throughout in OCR, Alsen opening visually checked; full book, interviews, statistics and legal/health claims not independently verified. Auntie Rita publisher descriptions and original-date metadata only: primary sample returned 403 even outside sandbox, and OverDrive sample URL was empty. Kooramindanjie body/preview inaccessible via OUP/JSTOR; coauthorship and section placement verified, not detailed argument. Public finding aid is metadata, not restricted manuscripts. Heiss review read fully, Sister Girl itself unread. Later edition/deposit dates are not backdated; selected cases do not represent all African American or Indigenous communities.
